transcript:
Header:
- Date/Time: 2026-10-08 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Miguel (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood Product), Nina (Lyra Head of ML), Omar (Lyra Eng Lead), Carla (Lyra SRE), Tom (Lyra Product)

Summary:
Redwood hosted API demo focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, common request parameters, retry/backoff behavior, and how Redwood Console surfaces streaming logs and token-level cost. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated/private for a consumer-facing finance assistant; primary concerns are latency (p50/p95), cost per 1M tokens, and data residency/security (KMS, audit logs). Next steps: pricing + security docs, performance benchmark with sample workload, and follow-up POC planning.

Topics:
- Quick intro + qualification
- Demo: simple chat flow -> system/user messages -> streaming tokens
- Parameters: temperature, max_tokens, stop, top_p, streaming chunk size, token limits
- Retries: idempotency keys, retryable error codes, exponential backoff, connection cut handling
- Console: live logs, streaming trace, cost breakdown per route
- Questions about privacy, KMS, retention, VPC
- Recap & next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, welcome, uh, from Redwood, I'm Aisha, account exec, I'll kick us off. Miguel and Jordan from our side, and on Lyra's side I see Nina, Omar, Carla, Tom. Can you all hear me okay?
[00:06] Nina: Yeah, loud and clear. Thanks.
[00:09] Omar: Yep, good to go.
[00:12] Aisha: Great. Quick agenda - 30 minute demo of Hosted API and Console focusing on chat and text gen basics, then 10-15 for questions and next steps. We know you're evaluating hosted vs dedicated/private; we want to show how streaming and retries work and how you can control params to trade latency vs cost.
[00:29] Miguel: Hi folks, I'll take the demo. I'll start with a simple chat flow, show streaming, then tweak params and show the Console traces. Quick note: transcription might have minor name mismatches in the call.
[00:40] Miguel: (screen share) Okay, here's our Playground - a small Node example calling /v1/chat/completions. First request: system prompt to set role, then user prompt asking for a brief financial summary. I'm going to set stream=true to show tokens as they're generated.
[01:00] Miguel: Sending now - you'll see first partial token at around 200ms in our dev region for this small prompt, p50 is usually 150-300ms depending on model and length.
[01:14] (short silence, keyboard clicking)
[01:17] Miguel: And there's the stream - 'The quarterly revenue improved...' etc, tokens arriving chunked. Carla: do you have any concerns about partial content showing to clients?
[01:28] Carla: We just want to make sure streaming doesn't leak PII if a request gets cut off or retried - retention and logs are important.
[01:35] Miguel: Totally - two notes: logs in Console can be redacted or configured, we also have per-route masking. Also streaming is stateless on our side per request; if connection drops you get partial content but you can re-request with idempotency key and resume pattern at client level. We do not persist streaming partials beyond traces unless logging enabled.
[01:50] Nina: And on retries, how do you handle duplicate tokens if client retries?
[01:55] Miguel: Good question. We recommend idempotency keys for non-streaming or when you need dedupe. For streaming, typical pattern is client buffers tokens locally; if the connection drops, issue a new request with the same idempotency key and server will return the same result if it was completed, or a consistent new result if the original didn't finish - depends on model determinism. We also provide deterministic sampling options (seed + temperature=0) for repeatability.
[02:20] Omar: How about params - which ones most affect latency vs quality?
[02:24] Miguel: Biggest levers: max_tokens and temperature/top_p. Higher max_tokens increases total latency linearly (more tokens to generate), temperature affects sampling variance not latency. We also recommend stopping early with 'stop' tokens if you can - that saves tokens and cost. Batch size at the request layer impacts throughput not single-request latency; we have continuous batching in the runtime that pools small requests to improve GPU efficiency but we expose config in Dedicated for strict latency SLOs.
[02:50] Tom: What's continuous batching - can it add jitter?
[02:52] Miguel: Yes, there's a small batching window; typical batch window is 10-30ms to gather requests. For high sensitivity you can pin to dedicated capacity or use lower batch windows. Hosted tier aims to balance cost vs latency.
[03:07] (Miguel types)
[03:12] Miguel: Now switching to console, here's the request trace. You can see streaming events, per-token timing, and cost estimate for this call. We also surface p50/p95 across routes and models.
[03:30] Nina: Nice, can you show token-level cost?
[03:33] Miguel: Sure - here's the breakdown: input tokens, output tokens, model unit price per 1k tokens. We also show cache hits if you enable prefix caching. For example this prompt had 12 input tokens, 78 output tokens - cost estimate shown.
[03:50] Omar: Does Redwood support retries client-side pattern examples?
[03:54] Miguel: Yes, our SDKs include retry helpers that automatically handle transient 5xx and connection errors with exponential backoff. We retry idempotent calls; for non-idempotent you should pass an idempotency key. We also expose retry budget config in the Console.
[04:12] Aisha: Quick qualification - what's your traffic profile and latency targets again Nina?
[04:17] Nina: We're expecting bursts to 200 rps for short prompts during peak trading hours, p95 latency target under 800ms, and soft requirement for data never leaving EWR region for EU customers - so residency & KMS are important.
[04:33] Miguel: Got it. For that shape, hosted API is possible but if you need strict residency and SLA-backed throughput, Dedicated or Private may be preferable; we can scope a Dedicated pool with reserved GPUs and VPC peering.
[04:48] Carla: Can you summarize security features for hosted? KMS, audit logs, SOC2?
[04:52] Miguel: We have SOC 2 Type II, optional customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations (bring-your-own-key on Dedicated and Private, hosted supports encrypted keys managed by us with Customer master key options), and audit logs with configurable retention in Console. I'll share the security pack after the call.
[05:10] (short pause)
[05:14] Miguel: Back to streaming mechanics - when stream=true, Redwood returns chunked events over the HTTP stream. Each event includes token text, token index, and partial probabilities if you enable debug mode. We don't persist the partials unless tracing/logging is enabled.
[05:32] Nina: For us it's important to limit token output in some cases - can we apply hard max_tokens per route and also enforce content filters?
[05:38] Miguel: Yes, you can set per-route policies: hard token caps, filters, and early stops. We also offer pre-output filters and post-output moderation hooks.
[05:46] Omar: You mentioned deterministic sampling - how strict is that? We need reproducible responses for some accounting flows.
[05:51] Miguel: Deterministic mode (seed + temp=0) will make generation deterministic for the same model binary and parameters - however model sharding/quantization differences can introduce variance. For legal/regulatory traces we recommend logging the prompt, model version, and seed along with response and storing hashes for audit.
[06:10] (keyboard)
[06:15] Jordan: Quick product note - Optimize (our cost/perf toolkit) can analyze your prompt set and recommend quantization and batching strategies to reduce cost for high-volume endpoints; it can also suggest caching policies.
[06:28] Nina: Can Optimize produce a before/after cost delta?
[06:30] Jordan: Yes, we run synthetic evals with your prompts and runtime profile and produce estimated cost savings and latency impact. It's usually accurate within 10-15% of real POC numbers.
[06:40] Omar: For retries again - what error codes are retryable?
[06:44] Miguel: We retry on network/connectivity faults and transient 5xx (502/503/504). We do not automatically retry on 4xx. For 409s or rate limits we surface a Retry-After header; SDKs honor that. Client-side idempotency keys are the recommended pattern for safe retries.
[06:58] Tom: If a stream connection drops after 60% of tokens, do you have a resume API or do we re-request?
[07:04] Miguel: There's no native resume token endpoint currently; typical pattern is to re-issue request with same idempotency key and our service will either return cached result if it completed or produce a new response. For long-running streams we recommend chunked output and storing partials client-side.
[07:22] (short laughter)
[07:24] Carla: Ok. A few more security specifics - will you share info on key rotation?
[07:28] Miguel: Yes, rotation policies differ by deployment type. Hosted uses managed key rotation; Dedicated/Private supports BYOK with rotation under your KMS. We'll include the exact rotation intervals in the security docs.
[07:41] Nina: Anything we should know about model versions and rollouts affecting determinism?
[07:46] Miguel: Model binary changes can change outputs. We support model pinning per-route so you can lock to a specific model version. Rollouts can be configured for canary or A/B, and the Console will show diffs and quality regressions if you connect evals.
[07:59] Omar: Can we get a demo of streaming with a larger prompt?
[08:02] Miguel: Sure - switching to a 400-token prompt and streaming. Note this will take longer; you'll see tokens come every ~40-60ms depending on model.
[08:18] (pause, typing)
[08:22] Miguel: Streaming large prompt... partials coming in - you can instrument at the client to show a spinner until first token, then stream text. For mobile clients we usually do first-token timeout display to improve UX.
[08:45] Nina: About cost - how do you bill partial streams? Is it output tokens only?
[08:50] Miguel: Billing is by token usage: input tokens + output tokens. Partial streaming doesn't create extra cost unless you re-request and generate more tokens. The Console shows the cost per call in near real-time.
[09:05] Tom: Do you expose per-customer quotas and rate limits?
[09:08] Miguel: Yes per API key you can apply rate limits and quotas; for enterprise we can do advanced throttling and quotas per sub-team.
[09:15] Carla: For logs and traces, how long are they kept?
[09:19] Miguel: Hosted default is 30 days, configurable up to 365 for paid plans; Dedicated/Private support customer-configured long-term retention. We'll include retention options in the security pack.
[09:30] (Miguel demonstrates Console charts)
[09:40] Miguel: Now a quick look at SDK code for retries - here's an example in Python and Node with exponential backoff and jitter. The SDK picks safe defaults but you can tune max_attempts and backoff factor.
[09:56] Omar: Are there any gotchas if we use HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1 for streaming?
[10:01] Miguel: We support both but streaming semantics differ slightly. HTTP/2 will multiplex streams and may have different connection management; the SDK hides most differences. For proxies, ensure they allow long-lived connections.
[10:16] Aisha: Quick pause - does anyone have additional must-haves before we move to wrap up?
[10:22] Nina: We'd like the benchmark to include p95 latency under load and cold start behavior. Also a cost estimate for 1M tokens/month.
[10:31] Aisha: Perfect - we'll include that in the benchmark scope.
[10:34] Miguel: One more thing on streaming chunk size: we expose a chunk_size param to control how many tokens per event in the HTTP stream; smaller chunks give lower initial latency but more network overhead. For mobile clients small chunks are better.
[10:49] Tom: Any limits on token size? We have some long system prompts.
[10:52] Miguel: There's a model- and plan-dependent token limit; hosted supports models up to 32k context on some variants. If you need more we can discuss Sharding/Context window strategies.
[11:05] (typing sounds)
[11:12] Miguel: Quick recap of recommended patterns: use streaming=true for UX, implement client buffering and first-token timeout, use idempotency keys for safe retries, enforce per-route max_tokens and stop tokens to cap cost, and use Optimize to recommend quantization/batching for high-volume endpoints.
[11:32] Aisha: Shall we outline the POC/benchmark next steps - who owns what?
[11:37] Omar: Lyra will provide sample prompt set and traffic profile, and an SRE contact for networking tests.
[11:43] Aisha: Redwood will send pricing and security docs and schedule the benchmark with Miguel leading the technical side.
[11:50] Nina: Sounds good. A couple more quick Qs - do you have any hardened PCI-like compliance? We handle payment flows and need strict controls.
[11:59] Miguel: Redwood isn't PCI-issuing service; we provide controls and audit logs, but for PCI environments we usually recommend Dedicated or Private deployment and we'll work through scoping. We'll follow up with compliance questionnaire.
[12:15] Tom: For SLA on hosted, what's the uptime and latency guarantee?
[12:19] Aisha: Hosted has best-effort SLAs; for contractual uptime and latency targets we move to Dedicated with SLA add-ons. We'll include SLA options in the follow-up.
[12:29] (pause)
[12:33] Miguel: Any final technical blockers?
[12:36] Nina: None immediate, just need the docs and benchmark.
[12:40] Omar: We'll also want to test timeouts and connection drop behavior in our mobile app environment.
[12:46] Miguel: Great - we can include a small test harness for simulated drops.
[12:51] Aisha: Okay, we'll wrap. Thanks everyone for your time. We'll share the deck, pricing, and security pack. Expect the docs by Monday.
[12:58] Nina: Thanks, appreciate it.
[13:01] Carla: Thanks all.
[13:03] Aisha: Bye!

End of call.
